# Preface {.unnumbered #sec-preface}

This book was written with Quirework, which is the software it is about.

I am aware of how that looks.
A book about a tool, made with the tool, is either a demonstration or a confession, and I have not decided which.

Quirework has no opinion about sentences.
It keeps a list of what a book has promised, reads the chapters against the list, and says so when one of them disagrees.
It said so several times while I was writing this one.
I fixed most of them.

If you find a place where this book disagrees with itself, you have found something the software missed.
I would like to hear about it, though not as much as you might think.

Every name in this book has been changed.

The rest is about a different book, and what I did instead of finishing it.

The preface is written and all five gates pass. Here it is, about 140 words:

> **Preface**
>
> This book was written with Quirework, which is the software it is about.
>
> I am aware of how that looks. A book about a tool, made with the tool, is either a demonstration or a confession, and I have not decided which.
>
> Quirework has no opinion about sentences. It keeps a list of what a book has promised, reads the chapters against the list, and says so when one of them disagrees. It said so several times while I was writing this one. I fixed most of them.
>
> If you find a place where this book disagrees with itself, you have found something the software missed. I would like to hear about it, though not as much as you might think.
>
> Every name in this book has been changed.
>
> The rest is about a different book, and what I did instead of finishing it.

What I did and didn't do:
- **Sidecar:** I removed the "no prose yet" note. Both of the preface's links to the spec still hold, so they're unchanged.
- **Spec:** No change. What you asked for is what the spec already says.
- **Not said:** The preface doesn't mention Full Stop's chapter count, Otto, Em, or how the book ends, so it doesn't step on later chapters or need the "eleven chapters" note.

These need your judgment:
- **"I fixed most of them."** It suggests the book still has disagreements in it. That's on purpose, but it's a claim about this book, so only keep it if you're happy to stand behind it.
- **The names line.** I left out your "exaggerated everything that deserved it" half to keep the line flat. Add it back if you'd rather have both.

**Before I start Two Shops:** your material has things a later writer could break. The main ones are that chapter four's title contains "fashionable", the week when both shops did it, and the rule that Two Shops shows the "where claims live" problem without saying it while Index Cards says it out loud. My plan is to put the "shows it, doesn't say it" rule in the guidance notes for both chapters. I'd also add the "fashionable" detail to the spec's two-shops section and record your words in the trail. Tell me if you'd rather keep the spec as it is.

Nothing is committed.

# Two Shops {#sec-two-shops}

Chapter four of Full Stop is about the dash, and its title is "A Fashionable Interruption."
I was proud of the title.
I will have to bring it up again later, and I will be less proud.

The argument of chapter four is that the dash did not spread on its own.
Marks rarely do.
Somebody has to set them in type, over and over, until readers stop noticing them and start expecting them.
In chapter four, that somebody is a printer's shop.
Its compositors liked the dash, used it where their neighbors used a comma or nothing at all, and printed enough popular books that within a generation every other shop was doing the same.
I had sources.
I had a paragraph about the shop's apprentices that I still think is the best thing I have written about anyone who handled lead for a living.

Chapter nine is about the semicolon.
The semicolon is a quieter mark with a worse reputation, and I gave it a sympathetic chapter, the way you sit next to the one person at a wedding nobody knows.
Halfway through, to explain why the semicolon lost ground when it did, chapter nine says the dash took it.
It also says who handed the dash over: a rival shop, across town, whose compositors set dashes where everyone else set semicolons, and who printed enough popular books that within a generation every other shop was doing the same.

I wrote chapter nine about a year after chapter four.
I had different sources by then.
I did not reread chapter four, because I had written it and knew what it said.

Red had read both chapters, and said nice things about each.

I won't name the shops.
They've suffered enough, and so have I.
Here they are the shop in chapter four and the shop in chapter nine, which is how I came to think of them anyway.

Fixing it looked easy.
One of the two chapters was wrong, or at least less right, and I only had to decide which.
I went back to the sources, decided chapter four was less right, and rewrote its last third so that its shop took up the dash early but the rival made it popular.
That was a smaller claim, and smaller claims are easier to defend.

Then I read chapter four through, and it no longer had an argument.
A chapter about a shop that was early to a fashion is a chapter about being early.
Nobody wants to read about being early.
So I gave chapter four its shop back and moved the doubt into chapter nine, where the rival now "helped popularize" the dash, a phrase that means nothing and that I typed anyway.

That left a hole in the middle of chapter nine where the semicolon's decline used to be explained.

That was the first round.
I am not going to say how many there were.
More than I told Hedda.
More than I will tell you.

Each fix needed a footnote in the other chapter.
If four gave its shop the credit, nine needed a note saying the rival's part was discussed in chapter four.
When four changed, the note in nine had to change, and the change in nine needed a note in four.
By the end the footnotes cited footnotes.
Note fourteen in chapter four said "but see note twenty-two in chapter nine," and note twenty-two in chapter nine said "for a qualification, see note fourteen in chapter four," and a careful reader could follow them for as long as a careful reader liked.

I printed both chapters and pinned them to the wall above my desk, four on the left and nine on the right, facing each other, like seconds at a duel.
It helped to see them at once.
I marked four in red pencil and nine in blue, and the places where they touched in purple, until there was more purple than either.

Then there was the week I decided both shops did it.

It came to me in the shower, which is where the best bad ideas come from.
Two shops in the same city, the same years, the same trade, the same customers.
Why not both?
Each could have taken up the dash on its own, independently, at the same time, the way two people at a dinner reach for the last roll.
Nobody had to be wrong.
Chapter four could keep its shop, chapter nine could keep its rival, and the footnotes could come down.

It was the happiest week of the book.
I took every footnote out.
I wrote a new paragraph for each chapter, nearly the same paragraph, saying that the dash had arrived in both shops at once, as ideas sometimes do.
I slept well.
When Hedda asked how the book was, I said "chapter four" with something close to pleasure.

On the seventh day I reread chapter four from the top, to enjoy it, and I started with the title.

"A Fashionable Interruption."

Fashion doesn't happen twice.

The footnotes went back up.
I had kept them, in a file called notes-old-DO-NOT-DELETE, which tells you how much I had believed in the week.

After that I stopped trying to win.
I tried instead to keep the two chapters from noticing each other.
I made chapter four vaguer about the date and chapter nine vaguer about the street.
I took the word "fashionable" out of the body of chapter four and left it in the title, where I could not bear to touch it.
Every change was small and every change was reasonable, and the chapters got harder to read and no easier to reconcile.

Then I half remembered a sentence in chapter two, which is about the comma, that mentioned a shop and a dash.
It was there.
It credited neither shop.
It credited "the printers of the period," which was safe, and which was also, now that I looked at it, a third position.

I pinned chapter two to the wall, to the left of four.
Chapter six had a line about the dash too, in a paragraph about the colon, so I pinned up six.
Chapter seven described the shop in chapter four in a way that fit the shop in chapter nine better.
I pinned up seven.

The seconds were no longer facing each other.
There were too many of them.

By spring I had run out of wall.

content.text:
Two Shops is written and all five gates pass. It's in `manuscript/sections/two-shops.qmd`, about 1,080 words. Nothing is committed.

**Preface:** The names line now reads: "Every name in this book has been changed, and everything that deserved it has been exaggerated." "I fixed most of them" stays.

**Two Shops, in order:**
- **The two chapters:** chapter four, "A Fashionable Interruption", credits one shop with making the dash fashionable. Chapter nine, on the semicolon, credits a rival. Neither shop is named; they're "the shop in chapter four" and "the shop in chapter nine". "They've suffered enough, and so have I" is in.
- **The rounds:** the first fix leaves chapter four without an argument, and putting it back opens a hole in nine. The rounds go uncounted: "More than I told Hedda. More than I will tell you."
- **The footnotes:** each fix needs one in the other chapter, ending with note fourteen and note twenty-two pointing at each other.
- **The wall:** four and nine pinned up facing each other like seconds at a duel, marked in red and blue pencil, with purple where they touch.
- **The happy week:** both shops did it independently. Then Cy rereads the title, and the chapter says only "Fashion doesn't happen twice."
- **The ending:** a sentence in chapter two credits "the printers of the period", which is a third position. Chapters six and seven go up on the wall too. The last lines are "The seconds were no longer facing each other. There were too many of them. By spring I had run out of wall." It never says the problem is where the claims live; that's left for Index Cards.

**Spec, guidance and trail, as agreed:**
- **Spec, two shops:** now has the footnotes citing footnotes, the happy week, and "fashionable" in chapter four's title.
- **Spec, claims in sentences:** now says Two Shops gets to the idea without saying it and Index Cards is the first to say it.
- **Spec, preface:** now has both halves of the names line, and says the book doesn't claim to be fully consistent.
- **Guidance notes:** the "doesn't say it" rule is in both chapters' notes, and the "named only by their chapters" rule is in Two Shops'. The preface's notes are updated to match.
- **Trail:** three new entries pointing at your turns in this session.

**Things for you to judge:**
- **Length:** it's about 220 words short of the target. That's room for any of your material you'd like given more space, or the slack can go to Index Cards.
- **New details I made up:** the title "A Fashionable Interruption" and the paragraph about the apprentices. Also the shower, the red and blue pencils, the file called notes-old-DO-NOT-DELETE, and what chapters two, six and seven say about the dash. Change whatever isn't true enough.
- **Red:** he gets one line, "Red had read both chapters, and said nice things about each." It's a quiet jab at nobody noticing. Cut it if he should stay out of this chapter.
- **Hedda:** she gets two passing mentions. I didn't link the chapter to the spec's section on the people who ask, because her answer is still "chapter four" and nothing about her changes here.

**Housekeeping:**
- **Wrapping:** `quirework dev check` first failed on line wrapping, so I ran `quirework text wrap` on the spec and the chapter. The tool asks for a wrap to be committed on its own, but all of this is new and uncommitted, so it can go in with the rest. The wrap joined "so have I." with the next sentence onto one source line. The rendered text is unaffected.
- **Capture this session:** the three new trail entries point at this conversation, which isn't captured yet. The trail check warns about that until you run `quirework provenance ingest claude`.

content:
That's the chapter. "Nobody wants to read about being early" is going on my wall, which I no longer have room on.

Keep everything you invented. "A Fashionable Interruption" is the title I'd have given it, and I'm annoyed again. The apprentices, the shower, the pencils, notes-old-DO-NOT-DELETE and chapters two, six and seven are all true now. Seven is the best: a chapter that agreed with the wrong shop without being asked.

Keep Red's one line. He did read both, and he did say nice things, in writing, which is worse.

Short is a house rule. Give the slack to Index Cards; it has the most to carry.

Commit it, then we're done for today.

The preface and Two Shops are committed as `1c50742`. All five checks passed before the commit, and nothing is left uncommitted.

Before committing I recorded today's decisions in the book:
- **Spec:** the section on the two shops now has the title "A Fashionable Interruption", chapter two's "the printers of the period", and chapter seven agreeing with the wrong shop without being asked. That way a later chapter can't quietly contradict them.
- **Trail:** there's a new entry for your turn keeping everything I invented.
- **Index Cards guidance:** it now gets about thirteen hundred words plus the roughly two hundred Two Shops left unused.

For you before the session ages out: four of the trail entries point at this conversation, which isn't captured yet. Run `quirework provenance ingest claude` when you're ready. Until then the trail check keeps warning about them, though it still passes. Whether to accept the captured session is up to you.
